Kinematics:
# Kinematics
## Describing motion
Distance is the total length of path travelled, a scalar. Displacement is the change in position in a given direction, a vector. Speed is the rate of change of distance; velocity is the rate of change of displacement. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
On a displacement–time graph the gradient is the velocity. On a velocity–time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area under the graph is the displacement.

## Uniform acceleration
For constant acceleration the suvat equations apply: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as and s = ½(u + v)t, where s is displacement, u initial velocity, v final velocity, a acceleration and t time. Near the Earth's surface, objects in free fall accelerate at g = 9.8 m s⁻² if air resistance is negligible.

## Projectiles
A projectile is an object moving under gravity alone after being launched. Its horizontal and vertical motions are independent: horizontal velocity is constant and vertical motion has acceleration g downwards. Air resistance reduces the range and maximum height and makes the path asymmetric. Terminal speed is the steady speed reached when drag equals weight.

## Key terms
Displacement: change in position in a given direction
Velocity: rate of change of displacement
Acceleration: rate of change of velocity
Projectile: an object moving under gravity alone
Terminal speed: the constant speed reached when drag equals weight
Forces and momentum:
# Forces and momentum
## Newton's laws
Newton's first law states that an object stays at rest or moves with constant velocity unless a resultant force acts on it. Newton's second law states that the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = ma for constant mass. Newton's third law states that when body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force of the same type on A.

## Types of force
Weight is the gravitational force on a mass, W = mg. The normal force is the contact force perpendicular to a surface. Friction opposes relative motion; static friction F ≤ μsN and dynamic friction F = μdN. Tension is the pulling force in a string. Drag is the resistive force on an object moving through a fluid. Upthrust is the upward force from a fluid. Hooke's law states that the extension of a spring is proportional to the force, F = −kx.

## Momentum and impulse
Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv, a vector. Impulse is the change in momentum, equal to force × time, and is the area under a force–time graph. In a closed system with no external forces, total momentum is conserved in collisions and explosions. In an elastic collision kinetic energy is also conserved; in an inelastic collision it is not.

## Circular motion
An object moving in a circle at constant speed accelerates towards the centre. Centripetal acceleration is a = v²/r = ω²r, and centripetal force is F = mv²/r. Angular velocity is the angle swept per unit time, ω = 2π/T.

## Key terms
Momentum: the product of mass and velocity
Impulse: force multiplied by time, equal to the change in momentum
Weight: the gravitational force on a mass
Normal force: the contact force perpendicular to a surface
Elastic collision: a collision in which kinetic energy is conserved
Centripetal force: the resultant force towards the centre in circular motion
Work, energy and power:
# Work, energy and power
## Work and energy
Work done is the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force, W = Fs cos θ. Energy is the capacity to do work, measured in joules. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, Ek = ½mv². Gravitational potential energy changes by ΔEp = mgΔh near the Earth. Elastic potential energy stored in a spring is ½kx².

## Conservation of energy
The principle of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between forms. In the absence of friction, mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) is conserved.

## Power and efficiency
Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy, P = W/t, measured in watts. For an object moving at constant velocity against a resistive force, P = Fv. Efficiency is the ratio of useful output energy (or power) to total input energy (or power). Energy density is the energy stored per unit volume of a fuel.

## Key terms
Work done: force multiplied by displacement in the direction of the force
Kinetic energy: the energy an object has because of its motion
Gravitational potential energy: the energy an object has because of its position in a gravitational field
Power: the rate of doing work
Efficiency: useful output energy divided by total input energy
Energy density: energy stored per unit volume
Rigid body mechanics:
# Rigid body mechanics
## Torque and equilibrium
Torque is the turning effect of a force, τ = Fr sin θ, where r is the distance from the axis. A rigid body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant torque on it are both zero. A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces that produce rotation without translation.

## Rotational motion
Angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration describe rotation, with equations matching the suvat equations. Moment of inertia is a measure of an object's resistance to angular acceleration, depending on how its mass is distributed about the axis, I = Σmr². Newton's second law for rotation is τ = Iα.

## Angular momentum and energy
Angular momentum is the product of moment of inertia and angular velocity, L = Iω. Angular momentum is conserved when no external torque acts, so a spinning skater who pulls in their arms spins faster. Rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω².

## Key terms
Torque: the turning effect of a force about an axis
Moment of inertia: resistance to angular acceleration
Angular momentum: moment of inertia multiplied by angular velocity
Couple: two equal, opposite forces that cause rotation only
Rotational equilibrium: zero resultant torque
Galilean and special relativity:
# Galilean and special relativity
## Reference frames
A reference frame is a coordinate system used to measure positions and times. An inertial reference frame is one that is not accelerating. Galilean relativity adds velocities simply: u′ = u − v. It fails at speeds close to the speed of light.

## Einstein's postulates
Einstein's postulates state that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all inertial observers. The Lorentz factor is γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).

## Consequences
Time dilation is the slowing of a moving clock: Δt = γΔt₀, where proper time Δt₀ is measured in the frame where the events happen at the same place. Length contraction is the shortening of a moving object along its direction of motion: L = L₀/γ, where proper length L₀ is measured at rest. Simultaneity is relative: events simultaneous in one frame may not be in another. Spacetime diagrams show worldlines; evidence for time dilation comes from muons reaching the Earth's surface.

## Key terms
Inertial frame: a reference frame that is not accelerating
Lorentz factor: γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)
Proper time: time measured in the frame where both events happen at the same place
Time dilation: moving clocks running slow
Length contraction: moving objects being shorter along their motion
Proper length: length measured at rest relative to the object
Thermal energy transfers:
# Thermal energy transfers
## Particles and temperature
Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles of a substance. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the temperature at which particles have minimum energy: T(K) = T(°C) + 273. Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of the particles in a substance. Density is mass per unit volume.

## Heating and changes of state
Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K, so Q = mcΔT. Specific latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance at constant temperature, so Q = mL. During a change of state the energy changes the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy.

## Energy transfer
Conduction is energy transfer by particle collisions through a material; the rate is ΔQ/Δt = kAΔT/Δx, where k is the thermal conductivity. Convection is energy transfer by the bulk movement of a fluid. Radiation is energy transfer by electromagnetic waves. A black body is an ideal absorber and emitter. The Stefan–Boltzmann law gives the power radiated as L = σAT⁴. Wien's displacement law states that λmax T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K.

## Key terms
Temperature: a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles
Internal energy: the total kinetic and potential energy of particles
Specific heat capacity: energy to raise 1 kg by 1 K
Specific latent heat: energy to change the state of 1 kg at constant temperature
Conduction: energy transfer by particle collisions
Black body: a perfect absorber and emitter of radiation
Greenhouse effect:
# Greenhouse effect
## Energy balance of the Earth
The solar constant is the intensity of the Sun's radiation at the Earth's distance, about 1360 W m⁻². Albedo is the fraction of incident radiation that a surface reflects. The Earth's average albedo is about 0.3. Emissivity is the ratio of the power radiated by a body to that radiated by a black body at the same temperature.

## The greenhouse effect
The greenhouse effect is the warming of the Earth's surface because greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation emitted by the surface and re-emit it, some back towards the surface. Greenhouse gases include water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide; their molecules absorb infrared because it makes them vibrate.

## Climate change
The enhanced greenhouse effect is the additional warming caused by increased greenhouse gas concentrations from human activity. Feedback effects, such as melting ice lowering albedo, can amplify warming. Energy balance models compare incoming solar power with outgoing radiated power to estimate the Earth's temperature.

## Key terms
Albedo: the fraction of incident radiation that is reflected
Emissivity: power radiated relative to a black body at the same temperature
Solar constant: the intensity of the Sun’s radiation at Earth, about 1360 W m⁻²
Greenhouse gas: a gas that absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation
Enhanced greenhouse effect: extra warming from human emissions
Gas laws:
# Gas laws
## Pressure and the mole
Pressure is force per unit area, p = F/A, measured in pascals. The mole is the amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of particles, NA = 6.02 × 10²³. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance.

## The gas laws
An ideal gas is a gas whose particles have negligible volume and no forces between them except during collisions. The equation of state for an ideal gas is pV = nRT, or pV = NkBT, where R is the gas constant and kB the Boltzmann constant. Boyle's law states that pressure is inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature. Charles's law states that volume is proportional to absolute temperature at constant pressure.

## Kinetic theory
Kinetic theory explains gas pressure as the result of particles colliding with the container walls. The average kinetic energy of a particle is proportional to absolute temperature: Ē = (3/2)kBT. Real gases behave like ideal gases at low pressure and high temperature.

## Key terms
Pressure: force per unit area
Mole: the amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles
Ideal gas: a gas obeying pV = nRT exactly
Boyle’s law: pressure inversely proportional to volume at constant temperature
Absolute zero: the temperature at which particles have minimum energy
Thermodynamics:
# Thermodynamics
## The first law
The first law of thermodynamics states that the heat added to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by the system: Q = ΔU + W. Work done by a gas at constant pressure is W = pΔV.

## Gas processes
An isobaric process happens at constant pressure. An isovolumetric process happens at constant volume. An isothermal process happens at constant temperature. An adiabatic process involves no heat transfer; for an ideal monatomic gas pV^(5/3) is constant. On a pV diagram, the area under the curve is the work done.

## The second law and entropy
The second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Entropy is a measure of the disorder of a system; ΔS = ΔQ/T. A heat engine converts heat into work using a cycle; its efficiency is useful work out divided by heat in. The Carnot cycle is the most efficient possible cycle, with efficiency 1 − Tc/Th.

## Key terms
First law of thermodynamics: Q = ΔU + W
Isothermal process: a process at constant temperature
Adiabatic process: a process with no heat transfer
Isobaric process: a process at constant pressure
Entropy: a measure of the disorder of a system
Carnot efficiency: the maximum efficiency, 1 − Tc/Th
Current and circuits:
# Current and circuits
## Charge and current
Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Δq/Δt, measured in amperes. Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points, V = W/q, measured in volts. Resistance is the ratio of potential difference to current, R = V/I, measured in ohms. Ohm's law states that current is proportional to potential difference for a conductor at constant temperature.

## Resistance and power
Resistivity is a property of a material: R = ρL/A. Electrical power is P = IV = I²R = V²/R. In series, resistances add: R = R₁ + R₂. In parallel, reciprocals add: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂. A potential divider uses resistors in series to provide a chosen fraction of a voltage.

## Cells and internal resistance
Electromotive force (emf) is the energy supplied by a source per unit charge. Internal resistance is the resistance inside a cell, so ε = I(R + r) and the terminal potential difference is less than the emf when current flows. Primary cells cannot be recharged; secondary cells can.

## Key terms
Electric current: the rate of flow of charge
Potential difference: energy transferred per unit charge
Resistance: potential difference divided by current
Resistivity: a material property: R = ρL/A
Electromotive force: energy supplied by a source per unit charge
Internal resistance: the resistance inside a cell
Simple harmonic motion:
# Simple harmonic motion
## Oscillations
An oscillation is a repeated back-and-forth motion about an equilibrium position. Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position: a = −ω²x. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. The period is the time for one complete oscillation; frequency is the number of oscillations per second, f = 1/T. Angular frequency is ω = 2πf.

## Examples
A mass on a spring oscillates with period T = 2π√(m/k). A simple pendulum, for small angles, has period T = 2π√(l/g). The period of SHM does not depend on the amplitude.

## Energy and phase
In SHM, energy is exchanged continuously between kinetic and potential energy while the total stays constant (with no damping). Maximum speed is v = ωx₀ at equilibrium. Phase difference describes how far one oscillation is ahead of another.

## Key terms
Simple harmonic motion: motion with acceleration proportional and opposite to displacement
Amplitude: maximum displacement from equilibrium
Period: time for one complete oscillation
Frequency: oscillations per second
Angular frequency: ω = 2πf
Phase difference: how far one oscillation is ahead of another
Wave model:
# Wave model
## Waves
A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy without transferring matter. A transverse wave has oscillations perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, such as light. A longitudinal wave has oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer, such as sound, with compressions and rarefactions.

## Describing waves
Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive points in phase. Frequency is the number of waves passing a point per second. The wave speed equation is v = fλ. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. Displacement–distance graphs show a wave at one instant; displacement–time graphs show one point over time.

## Electromagnetic waves
Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that travel through a vacuum at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. The electromagnetic spectrum, in order of increasing frequency, is radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Sound needs a medium and travels at about 340 m s⁻¹ in air.

## Key terms
Transverse wave: a wave with oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer
Longitudinal wave: a wave with oscillations parallel to energy transfer
Wavelength: the distance between consecutive points in phase
Wave speed: v = fλ
Electromagnetic spectrum: the range of electromagnetic waves from radio to gamma
Wave phenomena:
# Wave phenomena
## Reflection and refraction
Reflection is the bouncing back of a wave at a boundary; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Refraction is the change in direction of a wave as it changes speed when entering a new medium. The refractive index is n = c/v. Snell's law states that n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. The critical angle is the angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs; sin θc = n₂/n₁.

## Diffraction and interference
Diffraction is the spreading of a wave as it passes through a gap or around an obstacle; it is greatest when the gap is similar in size to the wavelength. Superposition is the adding of displacements when waves meet. Constructive interference happens when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths; destructive interference when it is a whole number plus half a wavelength.

## Double slit and gratings
In Young's double-slit experiment, fringe spacing is s = λD/d. A diffraction grating produces sharp maxima at angles given by nλ = d sin θ. Coherent sources have a constant phase difference and the same frequency.

## Key terms
Refraction: change of direction as a wave changes speed
Refractive index: n = c/v
Critical angle: the angle above which total internal reflection happens
Diffraction: spreading of a wave through a gap or round an obstacle
Superposition: adding the displacements of waves that meet
Coherent sources: sources with a constant phase difference and the same frequency
Standing waves and resonance:
# Standing waves and resonance
## Standing waves
A standing wave is formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency travelling in opposite directions. A node is a point of zero amplitude; an antinode is a point of maximum amplitude. Unlike a travelling wave, a standing wave does not transfer energy.

## Strings and pipes
For a string fixed at both ends and a pipe open at both ends, the fundamental has wavelength 2L, and all harmonics are possible. For a pipe closed at one end, the fundamental has wavelength 4L, and only odd harmonics are possible. Harmonics are frequencies that are whole-number multiples of the fundamental.

## Resonance and damping
Natural frequency is the frequency at which a system oscillates when left alone. Resonance is the large-amplitude oscillation that happens when a system is driven at its natural frequency. Damping is the loss of energy from an oscillating system, which reduces amplitude. Light damping gives a sharp resonance peak; heavy damping gives a broad, low peak. Critical damping returns a system to equilibrium fastest without oscillating.

## Key terms
Standing wave: a wave pattern from two opposite waves of the same frequency
Node: a point of zero amplitude
Antinode: a point of maximum amplitude
Harmonic: a whole-number multiple of the fundamental frequency
Resonance: large oscillations when driven at the natural frequency
Damping: loss of energy from an oscillating system
Doppler effect:
# Doppler effect
## The Doppler effect
The Doppler effect is the change in observed frequency of a wave when the source and observer move relative to each other. When the source moves towards the observer the waves are compressed, so the observed frequency is higher; when it moves away the frequency is lower.

## Sound
For a moving source, f′ = f v/(v ∓ us), using minus for approaching and plus for receding. For a moving observer, f′ = f (v ± uo)/v.

## Light
For light from sources moving much slower than light, Δf/f ≈ Δλ/λ ≈ v/c. Redshift is the increase in wavelength of light from a receding source; blueshift is the decrease for an approaching source. Redshift of galaxies is evidence that the universe is expanding. Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow, and radar measures vehicle speeds.

## Key terms
Doppler effect: change in observed frequency due to relative motion
Redshift: increase in wavelength from a receding source
Blueshift: decrease in wavelength from an approaching source
Gravitational fields:
# Gravitational fields
## Newton's law of gravitation
Newton's law of universal gravitation states that two point masses attract with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Kepler's laws describe planetary orbits: orbits are ellipses, equal areas are swept in equal times, and T² is proportional to r³.

## Fields
Gravitational field strength is the force per unit mass on a small test mass, g = F/m = GM/r². Field lines show the direction of the force. Gravitational potential is the work done per unit mass to bring a mass from infinity to a point, V = −GM/r. Gravitational potential energy is Ep = −GMm/r.

## Orbits and escape
For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force, so orbital speed is v = √(GM/r). Escape speed is the minimum speed needed to escape a gravitational field, v = √(2GM/r). Satellites experience drag in low orbits and gradually spiral inwards.

## Key terms
Gravitational field strength: force per unit mass
Gravitational potential: work done per unit mass to bring a mass from infinity
Escape speed: the minimum speed to escape a gravitational field
Orbital speed: v = √(GM/r) for a circular orbit
Kepler’s third law: T² is proportional to r³
Electric and magnetic fields:
# Electric and magnetic fields
## Electric fields
Electric charge is conserved and quantized in multiples of the elementary charge e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Coulomb's law states that the force between two point charges is F = kq₁q₂/r². Electric field strength is the force per unit positive charge, E = F/q. Between parallel plates the field is uniform: E = V/d. Electric potential is the work done per unit charge to bring a positive charge from infinity, V = kq/r.

## Magnetic fields
A magnetic field is a region where a magnet or moving charge feels a force. Magnetic field lines go from north to south outside a magnet. A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field in circles around it; the direction follows the right-hand grip rule. A solenoid produces a field like a bar magnet. Magnetic flux density is measured in teslas.

## Equipotentials
Equipotential surfaces join points of equal potential; no work is done moving a charge along one, and field lines cross them at right angles.

## Key terms
Electric field strength: force per unit positive charge
Coulomb’s law: F = kq₁q₂/r²
Electric potential: work done per unit charge to bring a charge from infinity
Equipotential: a surface of equal potential
Magnetic field: a region where a moving charge or magnet feels a force
Tesla: the unit of magnetic flux density
Motion in electromagnetic fields:
# Motion in electromagnetic fields
## Charges in electric fields
A charged particle in a uniform electric field experiences a constant force qE, so it accelerates uniformly. A charge accelerated through a potential difference V gains kinetic energy qV. A charge entering a field at right angles follows a parabolic path, like a projectile.

## Charges in magnetic fields
A charge moving through a magnetic field experiences a force F = qvB sin θ, perpendicular to both its velocity and the field. Because the force is perpendicular to the velocity, a charge moving at right angles to a uniform field moves in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB). The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is F = BIL sin θ, with direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule.

## Combined fields
In a velocity selector, crossed electric and magnetic fields let through undeflected only particles with speed v = E/B. Parallel wires carrying current exert forces on each other: attraction for currents in the same direction.

## Key terms
Magnetic force on a charge: F = qvB sin θ
Force on a current: F = BIL sin θ
Velocity selector: crossed fields that pass only particles with v = E/B
Fleming’s left-hand rule: the rule giving the direction of the force on a current in a field
Induction:
# Induction
## Magnetic flux
Magnetic flux is the product of magnetic flux density and the area perpendicular to it, Φ = BA cos θ, measured in webers. Flux linkage is the flux multiplied by the number of turns, NΦ.

## Faraday's and Lenz's laws
Faraday's law states that the induced emf is equal to the rate of change of flux linkage: ε = −NΔΦ/Δt. Lenz's law states that the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it, which is why there is a minus sign. A conductor of length L moving at speed v through a field B has an induced emf ε = BvL.

## Generators and transformers
An ac generator rotates a coil in a magnetic field, producing a sinusoidal emf. A transformer changes alternating voltages: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np for an ideal transformer. Step-up transformers increase voltage; step-down transformers decrease it. Electricity is transmitted at high voltage to reduce power losses in cables (P = I²R).

## Key terms
Magnetic flux: Φ = BA cos θ, measured in webers
Flux linkage: flux multiplied by the number of turns
Faraday’s law: induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage
Lenz’s law: an induced current opposes the change that causes it
Transformer: a device that changes alternating voltages
Structure of the atom:
# Structure of the atom
## Models of the atom
In the Geiger–Marsden–Rutherford experiment, alpha particles fired at gold foil mostly passed straight through, but a few were deflected through large angles, showing that the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, called nucleons. The nucleon number (mass number) A is the number of protons plus neutrons; the proton number (atomic number) Z is the number of protons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

## Energy levels and spectra
Electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels. When an electron moves to a lower level it emits a photon with energy equal to the difference between the levels, E = hf. An emission spectrum is a set of bright lines at specific wavelengths; an absorption spectrum is a set of dark lines in a continuous spectrum. Spectra identify elements, including in stars.

## The Bohr model
The Bohr model of hydrogen gives energy levels E = −13.6/n² eV, explaining the hydrogen spectrum. The nuclear radius is approximately R = R₀A^(1/3).

## Key terms
Nucleon: a proton or a neutron
Nucleon number: the number of protons plus neutrons
Proton number: the number of protons
Isotope: atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons
Emission spectrum: bright lines at the wavelengths an element emits
Absorption spectrum: dark lines where an element absorbs
Quantum physics:
# Quantum physics
## Photons
A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation with energy E = hf, where h is the Planck constant, 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The electronvolt is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of one volt, 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

## The photoelectric effect
The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of high enough frequency falls on it. The work function is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from a surface. The threshold frequency is the lowest frequency that causes emission. Einstein's equation is hf = Φ + Ek,max. The effect shows the particle nature of light, because the electron energy depends on frequency, not intensity.

## Wave–particle duality
Matter also behaves as waves. The de Broglie wavelength of a particle is λ = h/p. Electron diffraction is evidence for the wave nature of electrons. Compton scattering, the increase in wavelength of X-rays scattered by electrons, is evidence that photons carry momentum.

## Key terms
Photon: a quantum of electromagnetic radiation
Work function: the minimum energy to free an electron from a surface
Threshold frequency: the lowest frequency that causes photoelectric emission
de Broglie wavelength: λ = h/p
Electronvolt: the energy gained by an electron through 1 V, 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
Radioactive decay:
# Radioactive decay
## Types of radiation
Radioactive decay is the random, spontaneous emission of radiation from an unstable nucleus. Alpha particles are helium nuclei; they are highly ionizing and stopped by paper. Beta-minus particles are electrons emitted when a neutron changes into a proton, with an antineutrino; beta-plus decay emits a positron and a neutrino. Gamma rays are high-energy photons, weakly ionizing and very penetrating. Background radiation comes from natural and artificial sources around us.

## Decay equations
In alpha decay A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2. In beta-minus decay A is unchanged and Z rises by 1. Nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear equations.

## Half-life
Half-life is the time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay, or for the activity to halve. Activity is the number of decays per second, measured in becquerels. The decay constant λ is the probability of decay per unit time, related by T½ = ln 2/λ, and N = N₀e^(−λt). The strong nuclear force holds nucleons together at very short range.

## Key terms
Half-life: the time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay
Activity: the number of decays per second
Alpha particle: a helium nucleus
Beta-minus particle: an electron emitted from a nucleus
Gamma ray: a high-energy photon from a nucleus
Decay constant: the probability of decay per unit time
Background radiation: radiation always present from natural and artificial sources
Fission:
# Fission
## Mass defect and binding energy
Mass defect is the difference between the mass of the separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus. Binding energy is the energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons, equal to the mass defect times c² (E = mc²). Binding energy per nucleon is highest for iron-56, so nuclei near iron are the most stable.

## Fission
Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus, such as uranium-235, into two smaller nuclei and some neutrons, releasing energy. Fission is usually triggered by absorbing a slow neutron. A chain reaction happens when neutrons from one fission cause further fissions. Critical mass is the minimum mass of fuel needed to sustain a chain reaction.

## Nuclear reactors
In a nuclear reactor, the moderator slows neutrons so they can cause fission, control rods absorb neutrons to control the rate, and a coolant carries heat to a heat exchanger. Fuel enrichment increases the proportion of uranium-235. Radioactive waste must be stored safely for a long time.

## Key terms
Mass defect: the difference between the mass of separate nucleons and the nucleus
Binding energy: the energy needed to split a nucleus into nucleons
Fission: the splitting of a heavy nucleus
Chain reaction: a self-sustaining series of fissions
Moderator: material that slows neutrons in a reactor
Control rod: a rod that absorbs neutrons to control the reaction
Fusion and stars:
# Fusion and stars
## Fusion
Nuclear fusion is the joining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy because binding energy per nucleon increases. Fusion needs very high temperatures and pressures to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between nuclei. In the Sun, hydrogen fuses into helium.

## Stars
A star is stable when the outward radiation and gas pressure from fusion balance the inward gravitational force; this balance is called hydrostatic equilibrium. Luminosity is the total power radiated by a star, L = σAT⁴. Apparent brightness is the power received per unit area at the observer, b = L/(4πd²).

## The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram and stellar evolution
The Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram plots luminosity against surface temperature; most stars lie on the main sequence. Low-mass stars become red giants and then white dwarfs. High-mass stars become red supergiants, explode as supernovae and leave a neutron star or black hole. Stellar parallax measures distances to nearby stars: d (parsecs) = 1/p (arcseconds).

## Key terms
Fusion: the joining of light nuclei
Hydrostatic equilibrium: the balance between outward pressure and gravity in a star
Luminosity: the total power radiated by a star
Apparent brightness: power received per unit area
Main sequence: the band on the HR diagram where stars fuse hydrogen
Parsec: the distance at which a star shows a parallax of one arcsecond
